doc.title: Dick Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Fraternity life at DU and changing views of fraternities
summary: He was president of DU house, once a strong fraternity advocate, but later decided fraternities hurt students.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: And were you in a fraternity?
What was that life like? Different from fraternities today?

Oh gee I guess so. Yeah. It was, the world revolved around that. Now I was the president of the house. So I had some influence with them and I was a strong advocate of the fraternity system but I changed, Monk. As I grew older I grew more liberal and I became very sympathetic with those young men who were not invited to join fraternities and felt like second class citizens and I thought it was too harmful to them to be worth all that the fraternities brought. Yes they were good. But I am happy to see them become a thing of the past. I think they hurt the young people.
Did you have your meals right in the houses?

In the house. We had a professional cook but our own members were the waiters. It was very sociable, very pleasant. And I certainly was a big fan of fraternities until maybe the last ten years. I thought it over and changed my mind.
